title: Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI
authors: Tanuj Khattar, Nicholas C. Rubin, Craig Gidney, Michael Broughton, Guang Hao Low, Ryan Babbush
abstract: We discuss an effective paradigm of utilizing AI agents to better compile quantum circuits when one can constrain bottleneck subroutines to have some form of classically verifiable structure. For example, when critical subroutines are composed exclusively of reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement based uncomputation, one can efficiently simulate execution for classical inputs. This property facilitates efficient certification of approximate circuit synthesis via a form of fuzz testing, provided suitable assumptions on the input distribution. While this pattern was recently exploited to improve quantum cryptanalysis circuits, here we highlight the flexibility of the broader approach by discussing three important applications. (1) The computation of $1/\sqrt{x}$ that bottlenecks real space simulations of the Coulomb operator such as those important for modeling inertial confinement fusion reactors. (2) The decoding of Reed-Solomon codes which bottlenecks the decoded quantum interferometry algorithm when used to approximately solve the optimal polynomial intersection problem. And (3) the quantum look-up tables and controlled application of Givens rotations that bottleneck the most performant quantum algorithms for simulating chemistry in second quantization. We discuss reference implementations of these algorithms and how they can be constrained and verified in the interest of seeding a Kaggle competition designed to accelerate AI-based research into the optimization of their compilation.
summary: This paper proposes a novel compilation paradigm where AI agents optimize quantum circuits by restricting bottleneck subroutines to have a classically verifiable structure. This allows for efficient classical simulation and rigorous testing of approximate circuit correctness. The approach is demonstrated across three critical quantum applications, aiming to accelerate the field through a public competition.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently compiling complex quantum circuits, particularly those containing resource-intensive subroutines.
main_result: By constraining bottleneck subroutines to possess a classically verifiable structure (e.g., reversible classical logic), the authors enable efficient classical simulation and certification of approximate circuit synthesis.
method: The core method involves using AI agents to guide compilation, leveraging techniques like fuzz testing based on the Fiat-Shamir heuristic to verify approximate correctness on sampled inputs.
model_or_system: The work focuses on abstract quantum circuits and computational models, demonstrated through applications like simulating the Coulomb operator for fusion, decoding Reed-Solomon codes, and simulating chemistry in second quantization.
key_observables: Fidelity of the purified output state, failure rate $\epsilon$, and the estimated Toffoli count (CBE) for circuit encoding.
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($n_p$), the error rate $\epsilon$, and the structure of the subroutines (e.g., kickmix gates).
main_assumptions: The classical verification only guarantees high fidelity if approximate correctness on sampled basis states implies high fidelity on the actual quantum states, and the simulation assumes specific input distributions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the paradigm, details the 'kickmix' gate set and simulation capabilities, and then applies this framework to three specific, complex computational benchmarks (fusion, coding, chemistry) to seed a Kaggle competition.
why_interesting: The focus on verifiable structure and classical simulation techniques for quantum computation is highly relevant for developing practical, resource-aware quantum algorithms and compilers.
